title: Porosity, Air-Filled Porosity, and Water-Holding Capacity
objective: Measure the air-water framework of a substrate and explain why the same mix behaves differently in different containers.

terms.definition: Fraction of bulk substrate volume occupied by pores.
Water retained after saturation and free drainage in a specific container.
Pore volume filled with air at container capacity.
Saturated or near-saturated layer retained above the container base by capillary forces.

coreScience: Container substrates are three-phase systems made of solids, liquid water, and gas-filled pore space. Total porosity describes how much of the container volume is pore space, but it does not tell the grower how that pore volume is divided between water and air after irrigation and drainage. Large, well-connected pores tend to empty at relatively low suction and refill with air; smaller pores retain water more strongly. Two media can therefore have similar total porosity yet create very different root-zone oxygen supply, water storage, and irrigation frequency.

Container capacity is a system property, not just a bag-of-media property. After saturation and free drainage, capillary forces retain water in part of the pore network. The vertical height of the substrate column changes the average water-to-air distribution: in general, a taller column of the same uniformly packed substrate contains a larger proportion of drained, air-filled pore space than a shallow column. Adding more holes can improve drainage pathways and prevent a blocked outlet, but it does not erase the capillary pressure relationships that create the retained-water profile inside the medium.

Physical properties also change during the crop. Organic particles can swell, shrink, and decompose; fine particles can migrate; roots can occupy or redirect pore space; repeated irrigation can settle the mix; salts, precipitates, and biofilms can alter hydraulic pathways; and handling or top-watering can compact material. A fresh-media specification is therefore a starting measurement rather than a guarantee of end-of-cycle behavior. Comparisons are most useful when container geometry, packing, saturation procedure, drainage time, and measurement method are kept consistent.

Air space, water-filled pore space, and total porosity should be interpreted together with irrigation behavior. A medium with high water storage may be useful in one crop or container but risky when irrigation is too frequent, root respiration is high, or drainage is poor. A highly aerated medium can reduce the duration of saturation but may require more frequent irrigation and tighter control of hydraulic uniformity. The goal is not to maximize one physical property; it is to match the air-water balance to plant size, root occupancy, container dimensions, climate, and irrigation strategy.
cultivationRelevance: Use physical-property measurements to choose and manage media rather than relying on labels such as “light,” “airy,” or “well draining.” Compare the same substrate in the actual container size and packing method used for production. When changing from seedling cells to larger containers, or from hand watering to high-frequency drip, expect the useful air-water balance and irrigation interval to change even if the media recipe does not.

When plants show slow dryback, persistent saturation, uneven wilt, weak root development, or large differences between containers, inspect the physical system before treating the symptom as a nutrient problem. Check settling, compaction, root occupancy, channeling, blocked drainage, container height, irrigation distribution, and changes in media structure. Physical measurements are especially valuable when a new media lot or container design performs differently from the previous crop.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record measured internal container volume, substrate height, top and bottom diameter where relevant, base shape, drainage-hole number and location, and whether liners, saucers, fabric walls, benches, or other features can restrict drainage or evaporation. Keep the same container geometry when comparing media batches.

Record media brand or recipe, lot, component ratios, initial moisture condition, particle-size observations where available, fill mass or bulk-density method, packing/compaction procedure, and whether the material was pre-wetted. Small changes in packing can change pore distribution enough to make comparisons misleading.

Using a documented method, record the container volume, water required to reach saturation, drainage time, drained-water volume, retained-water estimate, calculated total porosity, calculated air space, and calculated water-filled pore space or container capacity. Report the denominator and method with every percentage so values from different procedures are not mixed.

At defined crop stages, record settling or shrinkage, surface crusting, root occupancy, visible channeling, compaction, decomposition, algae or biofilm, and any change in drainage time. If performance changes materially, repeat the same physical test with the same procedure rather than assuming the fresh-media value still applies.

Pair physical-property data with irrigation volume, event frequency, runoff or drainage fraction where used, time to drain, dryback trend, spatial uniformity, root-zone moisture measurements when available, and plant response. Interpret the media as part of a coupled container-irrigation-root system rather than as an isolated material.

misconceptions: More perlite always means perfect aeration: Particle size, proportion, packing, container height, root occupancy, and irrigation determine the final air-water behavior; an ingredient name alone does not establish air space.

More drainage holes remove perched water: Additional outlets can prevent blockage and speed exit from the base, but they do not eliminate the capillary forces that retain water inside the substrate profile.
Water-holding capacity is a property of the bag alone: Container height, packing, saturation history, drainage time, root growth, and the measurement method affect the observed value.

Maximum water storage is always best for the plant: More retained water can lengthen irrigation intervals, but it can also reduce gas-filled pore space and extend saturation when the system is poorly matched to crop demand.
evidenceLimits: Physical-property values depend on the test method, container dimensions, packing, saturation procedure, drainage interval, temperature, and media condition. Different laboratories and extension methods may use related but nonidentical definitions or denominators, so percentages should not be compared without checking methodology. Most published container-substrate procedures are general horticulture evidence rather than cannabis-specific performance thresholds; use them to measure the root-zone system, not to claim a universal cannabis target.
